questions.question: Where did many of the Viking settle after they got defeated?
questions.explanation: The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in England united under King Alfred the Great, who defeated the Vikings. Many of the Viking invaders stayed in Britain - especially in the east and north of England, in an area known as the Danelaw (many places names there, such as Grimsby and Scunthorpe, come from the Viking languages).

questions.question: What was the Spanish Armada?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth became one of the most popular monarchs in English history, particularly after 1588, when the English defeated the Spanish Armada (a large fleet of ships), which had been sent by Spain to conquer England and restore Catholicism.

questions.question: When were the last Welsh rebellions defeated?
questions.explanation: By the middle of the 15th century the last Welsh rebellions had been defeated. English laws and the English language were introduced.

questions.question: What was 'Shampooing' when it was first introduced?
questions.option_a: The Indian art of head massage
questions.explanation: Mahomet and his wife also introduced 'shampooing', the Indian art of head massage, to Britain.

questions.question: What was the 'Black Death'?
questions.explanation: In 1348, a disease, probably a form of plague, came to Britain. This was known as the Black Death. One third of the population of England died and a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.

questions.question: What helped the progress of the industrial revolution?
questions.explanation: Scientific discoveries, such as James Watt's work on steam power, helped the progress of the Industrial Revolution.

questions.question: How many American colonies declared their independence in 1776?
questions.explanation: In 1776, 13 American colonies declared their independence, stating that people had a right to establish their own governments. The colonists eventually defeated the British army and Britain recognised the colonies' independence in 1783.

questions.question: Which of the events is the bombing of English cities by the Germans?
questions.explanation: The Blitz was the German air force bombing London and other British cities at night-time. The phrase 'the Blitz spirit' is still used today to describe Britons pulling together in the face of adversity.

questions.question: What did the Romans introduce to Britain?
questions.explanation: The Romans remained in Britain for 400 years. They built roads and public buildings, created a structure of law, and introduced new plants and animals.

questions.question: Who was the first Danish King?
questions.explanation: The first Danish King was Cnut, also called Canute.

questions.question: What is the period after the Norman Conquest up until 1485 called?
questions.explanation: The period after the Norman Conquest up until about 1485 is called the Middle Ages or the medieval period. It was a time of almost constant war.

questions.question: When were the women given the right to vote at the same age as men?
questions.explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst was born in Manchester in 1858. She set up the Women's Franchise League in 1889, which fought to get the vote in local elections for married women. Shortly before Emmeline's death in 1928, women were given the right to vote at the age of 21, the same as men.

questions.question: Which party did Margaret Thatcher belong to?
questions.explanation: Margaret Thatcher, Britain's first woman Prime Minister, led the Conservative government from 1979 to 1990.

questions.question: How long is the Bayeux Tapestry?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Hastings is commemorated in a great piece of embroidery, known as the Bayeux Tapestry which is 70 meters long.

questions.question: What was the purpose of the Corn Laws in 1846?
questions.option_a: To prevent the import of cheap grain
questions.explanation: Corn Laws in 1846 had prevented the import of cheap grain

questions.question: Who were the first people to start living in Britain?
questions.explanation: The first people to live in Britain were hunter-gatherers, in what we call the Stone Age.

questions.question: When did the English defeat the Spanish Armada?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth became one of the most popular monarchs in English history, particularly after 1588, when the English defeated the Spanish Armada (a large fleet of ships), which had been sent by Spain to conquer England and restore Catholicism.

questions.question: What were the working conditions like during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explanation: Working conditions during the Industrial Revolution were very poor. There were no laws to protect employees, who were often forced to work long hours in dangerous situations. Children also worked and were treated in the same way as adults.

questions.question: When did Britain become separated from the continent?
questions.explanation: Britain only became permanently separated from the continent by the Channel about 10,000 years ago.

questions.question: Which of Henry VIII's wives were executed?
questions.option_a: Catherine Parr and Anne of Cleves
questions.option_b: Catherine of Aragon and Anne Boleyn
questions.option_d: Anne of Cleves and Jane Seymour
questions.explanation: Anne Boleyn was English. She and Henry had one daughter, Elizabeth. Anne was unpopular in the country and was accused of taking lovers. She was executed at the Tower of London. Catherine was a cousin of Anne Boleyn. She was also accused of taking lovers and executed.

questions.question: When was the first coin in Britain made?
questions.explanation: The Iron Age people made the first coins to be minted in Britain, some inscribed with the names of Iron Age kings.

questions.question: Where was one of the Anglo Saxon kings buried with treasure and armour?
questions.explanation: The burial place of one of the kings was at Sutton Hoo in modern Suffolk. This king was buried with treasure and armour, all placed in a ship which was then covered by a mound of earth. Scotland and Wales remained free of Anglo Saxon rule.

questions.question: When did the Habeas Corpus Act become law?
questions.explanation: The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679. This was a very important piece of legislation which remains relevant today. Habeas corpus is Latin for 'you must present the person in court'. The Act guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully. Every prisoner has a right to a court hearing.

questions.question: When did English become the official language for documents?
questions.explanation: By 1400, in England, official documents were being written in English, and English had become the preferred language of the royal court and Parliament.

questions.question: What was the estimated population of the British Empire?
questions.explanation: During the Victorian period, the British Empire grew to cover all of India, Australia and large parts of Africa. It became the largest empire the world has ever seen, with an estimated population of more than 400 million people.

questions.question: Why was Mary known as 'Bloody Mary'?
questions.option_b: She put her sister in prison
questions.explanation: Mary was a devout Catholic and persecuted Protestants.

questions.question: How many Houses did the Scottish Parliament have in the middle ages?
questions.explanation: In the middle ages the Scottish Parliament had three Houses, called Estates: the lords, the commons and the clergy.

questions.question: When did the English Civil war begin?
questions.explanation: Civil war between the king and Parliament began in 1642. The country split into those who supported the king (the Cavaliers) and those who supported Parliament (the

questions.question: What event is known as the evacuation of 300,000 people from the beaches?
questions.explanation: Many civilian volunteers in small pleasure and fishing boats from Britain helped the Navy to rescue more than 300,000 men from the beaches around Dunkirk. The evacuation gave rise to the phrase 'the Dunkirk spirit'.

questions.question: What did the Chartists campaign for?
questions.option_a: Anyone to be able to stand as an MP
questions.option_c: Every man to have a vote
questions.explanation: In the 1830s and 1840s, a group called the Chartists campaigned for reform. They wanted six changes: for every man to have the vote;elections every year;for all regions to be equal in the electoral system; secret ballots; for any man to be able to stand as an MP; for MPs to be paid.

questions.question: Where was William Shakespeare born?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare (1564-1616) was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England.

questions.question: Who developed important Economics ideas?
questions.explanation: Many of the great thinkers of the Enlightenment were Scottish. Adam Smith developed ideas about economics which are still referred to today.

questions.question: What county does Stonehenge stand in?
questions.explanation: Stonehenge, still stands in what is now the English county of Wiltshire. Stonehenge was probably a special gathering place for seasonal ceremonies.

questions.question: What does the York Minster have?
questions.explanation: York Minster had windows of stained glass, telling stories about the Bible and Christian saints.

questions.question: What is Richard Arkwright remembered for?
questions.explanation: Born in 1732, Arkwright originally trained and worked as a barber. He was able to dye hair and make wigs. When wigs became less popular, he started to work in textiles. He improved the original carding machine. Arkwright is particularly remembered for the efficient and profitable way that he ran his factories.

questions.question: The Civil War in 1642 split the country into which two groups?
questions.option_c: House of York and House of Lancaster
questions.option_d: House of Commons and House of Lords
questions.explanation: Civil war between the king and Parliament could not now be avoided and began in 1642. The country split into those who supported the king (the Cavaliers) and those who supported Parliament (the Roundheads).

questions.question: When did the Enlightenment happen?
questions.explanation: During the 18th century, new ideas about politics, philosophy and science were developed. This is often called 'the Enlightenment'.

questions.question: Where can you find the ship HMS Victory now?
questions.explanation: HMS Victory, can be visited in Portsmouth. It was Admiral Nelson's ship.

questions.question: Who was the first woman Prime Minister?
questions.explanation: In 1979, Margaret Thatcher became the first woman Prime Minister of the UK. She was the longest-serving Prime Minister of the 20th century, remaining in Office until 1990.

questions.question: Who designed the Clifton Suspension Bridge?
questions.explanation: Brunel was originally from Portsmouth, England. He was an engineer who built tunnels, bridges, railway lines and ships. He was responsible for constructing the Great Western Railway and the Clifton Suspension Bridge.

questions.question: Who ordered to write the Book of Common Prayer?
questions.explanation: Henry VIII was succeeded by his son Edward VI, who was strongly Protestant. During his reign, the Book of Common Prayer was written to be used in the Church of England.

questions.question: Which clan was killed because of not taking an oath?
questions.explanation: All Scottish clans were required formally to accept William as king by taking an oath. The MacDonalds of Glencoe were late in taking the oath and were all killed.

questions.question: Who lost a lot of their power after the Battle of Culloden in 1746?
questions.explanation: The clans lost a lot of their power and influence after Culloden. Chieftains became landlords if they had the favour of the English king, and clansmen became tenants who had to pay for the land they used.

questions.question: Which country(s) did Britain fight against during the Battle of Trafalgar?
questions.explanation: Britain's navy fought against combined French and Spanish fleets, winning the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805.

questions.question: What treaty was signed in 1707?
questions.option_c: The Act for Government of Wales
questions.explanation: The Act of Union, known as the Treaty of Union in Scotland, was therefore agreed in 1707, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain.

questions.question: Who is known as William the Conqueror?
questions.explanation: In 1066, an invasion led by William, the Duke of Normandy (in what is now northern France), defeated Harold, the Saxon king of England, at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed in the battle. William became king of England and is known as William the Conqueror.

questions.question: What is the 'Divine Right of Kings'?
questions.option_a: The King was Appointed by God
questions.option_b: Reduced the power of the nobles
questions.option_c: Reduced the power of the King
questions.explanation: Divine Right of Kings' is the idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule. The king should be able to act without having to seek approval from Parliament.

questions.question: What were the refugees that came from France called?
questions.explanation: Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came from France. They were Protestants and had been persecuted for their religion.

questions.question: When did the Romans successfully invade Britain?
questions.explanation: Julius Caesar led a Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC. This was unsuccessful and for nearly 100 years Britain remained separate from the Roman Empire. In AD 43 the Emperor Claudius led the Roman army in a new invasion. This time, there was resistance from some of the British tribes but the Romans were successful in occupying almost all of Britain.

questions.question: Which Castles are in use to this day?
questions.explanation: Castles were built in many places in Britain and Ireland, partly for defence. Today many are in ruins, although some, such as Windsor and Edinburgh, are still in use.

questions.question: Who was the 'Iron Duke' that defeated the Emperor Napoleon?
questions.explanation: In 1815, the French Wars ended with the defeat of the Emperor Napoleon by the Duke of Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo. Wellington was known as the Iron Duke and later became Prime Minister.

questions.question: During Slave trade, where did slaves primarily come from?
questions.explanation: Slaves came primarily from West Africa. Travelling on British ships in horrible conditions, they were taken to America and the Caribbean, where they were made to work on tobacco and sugar plantations.

questions.question: What tools did the Bronze age people introduce?
questions.explanation: The people of the Bronze Age were accomplished metalworkers who made many beautiful objects in bronze and gold, including tools, ornaments and weapons.

questions.question: How many colonies were granted independence in 1947?
questions.explanation: Another aspect of change was self-government for former colonies. In 1947, independence was granted to nine countries, including India, Pakistan and Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). Other colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific achieved independence over the next 20 years.

questions.question: When did the Irish Free State become a republic?
questions.explanation: In 1922 Ireland became two countries. The six counties in the north which were mainly Protestant remained part of the UK under the name Northern Ireland. The rest of Ireland became the Irish Free State. It had its own government and became a republic in 1949.

questions.question: What is meant by 'common law'?
questions.option_d: Sentence is decided by the jury
questions.explanation: In England, judges developed 'common law' by a process of precedence (that is, following previous decisions) and tradition. In Scotland, the legal system developed slightly differently and laws were 'codified' (that is, written down).

questions.question: What became the symbol of the House of Tudor?
questions.explanation: This war was called the Wars of the Roses, because the symbol of Lancaster was a red rose and the symbol of York was a white rose. The war ended with the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 the House of Lancaster won. The symbol of the House of Tudor was a red rose with a white rose inside it as a sign that the Houses of York and Lancaster were now allies.

questions.question: When were women given the right to vote at the same age as men?
questions.explanation: In 1918, women over the age of 30 were given voting rights and the right to stand for Parliament, partly in recognition of the contribution women made to the war effort during the First World War. Shortly before Emmeline's death in 1928, women were given the right to vote at the age of 21, the same as men.

questions.question: When was The First British Prime minister (Sir Robert Walpole) in power?
questions.explanation: The first man to be called 'Prime Minister' was Sir Robert Walpole, who was Prime Minister from 1721 to 1742.

questions.question: Who was Isambard Kingdom Brunel?
questions.explanation: Brunel was originally from Portsmouth, England. He was an engineer who built tunnels, bridges, railway lines and ships.

questions.question: When did the Industrial Revolution take place?
questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution was the rapid development of industry in Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries.

questions.question: Where can you visit Admiral Nelson's ship , HMS Victory?
questions.explanation: Admiral Nelson's ship, HMS Victory, can be visited in Portsmouth

questions.question: Which house won the War of the Roses?
questions.explanation: The war ended with the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485. King Richard III of the House of York was killed in the battle and Henry Tudor, the leader of the House of Lancaster, became King Henry VII.
